text:
The bunkering operation took place on May 23, 2026, and represents an important step milestone in the efforts to advance practical low-emission fuel solutions for the shipping industry. Since the operation, the Eco Levant has been running on a blended ethanol-methanol marine fuel.

As explained, the fuel mixture consisted of 90% ISCC EU-certified biomethanol and 10% ISCC EU-certified second-generation ethanol. According to the company, the bunkering was carried out safely under controlled operational conditions.

While methanol bunkering is already an established practice, the introduction of ethanol marks a notable development. During the operation, the ethanol and methanol were supplied separately to the vessel by a single inland bunker barge. The two fuels were then blended onboard the receiving vessel.

Maritime fuels continue to evolve. At X-Press Feeders, we believe it’s essential to continue to evaluate workable solutions and develop them further — solutions that contribute to reducing our fleet’s emissions.

title: Canaries achieve Brussels' support to extend the ETS exemption until at least 2040
description:
This exemption, which is currently in force until 2030 as an exception to the general EU regulation, is considered key to the archipelago's connectivity.
This was stated by the Canarian president, Fernando Clavijo, during the plenary session of the regional Parliament.
In this regard, Clavijo explained that during a recent visit to Brussels, where he met with the team of the Commissioner for Climate and for Transport and Tourism, he was assured of "support" to extend the current exception to the European emissions trading system (ETS) over time.
The president's words were in response to a question raised by deputy Raúl Acosta (AHI), who was interested in the steps the regional Executive is taking for the EU to relax the emissions trading scheme, with special attention to maritime transport.
This area, he recalled, is "under review" within the Union, and any exemption or relief for the Canary Islands would have a direct "final impact" on the cost borne by the residents of the archipelago.
text:
The Government of the Canary Islands has defended before European institutions the need to keep inter-island flights and air routes with the Peninsula exempt from the payment of CO2 emission rights, at least until 2040, taking advantage of its status as an Outermost Region (OR). This exemption, which is currently in force until 2030 as an exception to the general EU regulation, is considered key to the archipelago's connectivity.

This was stated by the Canarian president, Fernando Clavijo, during the plenary session of the regional Parliament. The head of the Executive stressed that, although it is essential to make an "important effort" to reduce polluting emissions and "be much more respectful" of the environment, the specific situation of the Canary Islands as an outermost territory grants it "a legal umbrella" in Article 349 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU, which would allow "to modulate" the application of European climate policy.

In this regard, Clavijo explained that during a recent visit to Brussels, where he met with the team of the Commissioner for Climate and for Transport and Tourism, he was assured of "support" to extend the current exception to the European emissions trading system (ETS) over time.

The president's words were in response to a question raised by deputy Raúl Acosta (AHI), who was interested in the steps the regional Executive is taking for the EU to relax the emissions trading scheme, with special attention to maritime transport. This area, he recalled, is "under review" within the Union, and any exemption or relief for the Canary Islands would have a direct "final impact" on the cost borne by the residents of the archipelago.

Acosta warned of the economic consequences that a strict application of these payments could entail in territories like El Hierro: "If, even with the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, prices have skyrocketed, in El Hierro, this would mean putting a noose around our necks. Here there are two different but complementary issues: on the one hand, the validity of that exemption beyond 2030 and also the need to relax or limit these payments also in the case of routes between Canarian ports and the rest of the ports of the European Union."

text:
Coordinated by the Norwegian maritime cluster Maritime CleanTech, the 30-month EU-funded project officially kicked off in Brussels on May 20–21, 2026. Backed by nearly €2 million under the Horizon Europe programme, SeaThrive aims to help early-stage fuel concepts move from initial ideas to investment-ready projects.

The project targets one of the key bottlenecks in maritime decarbonization: the difficulty of turning promising low- and zero-emission fuel concepts into bankable business cases. It will provide hands-on support through training sessions, workshops, advisory services and matchmaking between stakeholders.

Over its lifetime, SeaThrive plans to run more than 15 workshops across Europe, reach over 10,000 participants through online training and support more than 20 project proposals towards funding opportunities.

A major component of the initiative is the development of an advanced financial analysis tool designed specifically for alternative fuel projects. The tool will help stakeholders assess total costs including CAPEX, OPEX and regulatory compliance, and better understand operational impacts, risks and revenue potential.

SeaThrive aims to move promising fuel projects from early uncertainty to investment-ready decisions by combining better tools with hands-on project support

… said Håvard Tvedte, Interim CEO of Maritime CleanTech.

SeaThrive also aims to strengthen Europe’s broader maritime innovation ecosystem by connecting industry, research institutions and maritime clusters. Partners include regional clusters from France, Italy and Germany, as well as research organisations such as National Technical University of Athens, VTT Technical Research Centre of Finland and Maersk Mc-Kinney Moller Center for Zero Carbon Shipping, alongside industry and SME participants.

The consortium also plans to develop a “living lab” digital platform to support ongoing collaboration.

title: IMO adopts MASS Code and guidelines for alternative fuels - WorldCargo News
description:
IMO has advanced the MASS Code and ammonia fuel guidelines to support safer autonomous shipping and the adoption of new technologies and alternative fuels.
The MASS Code applies to cargo ships covered under SOLAS Chapter 1.
Roadmap towards binding rules The new MASS Code supplements existing IMO instruments, taking into account international law, including the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS).
The next steps for the Code include: December 2026 – MSC 112 to re-establish MASS Working Group for the Development of a framework for an Experience-Building Phase (EBP) of the non-mandatory MASS Code; 2028 – Development of the mandatory MASS Code, based on the non-mandatory Code and results from the EBP and review conducted by the relevant sub-committees.
Guidelines for ships using alternative fuels Additionally, the Committee continued work on the safety regulatory framework for ships using new technologies and alternative fuels.
text:
IMO has advanced the MASS Code and ammonia fuel guidelines to support safer autonomous shipping and the adoption of new technologies and alternative fuels.

The MASS Code sets out a comprehensive, goal-based framework to ensure that remotely controlled or autonomous ships are designed and operated to a level of safety, security, and environmental protection expected of a conventional ship. They will also be required to comply with the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea (SOLAS) and other applicable mandatory instruments of the IMO.

The Code applies to cargo ships and will take effect from 1 July 2026. As it is a non-mandatory instrument, Member States are allowed to test its use while paving the way for making it mandatory under the SOLAS Convention. The MASS Code applies to cargo ships covered under SOLAS Chapter 1.

Welcoming the milestone at the conclusion of the 111th session of the Maritime Safety Committee (MSC) in London, held 13 to 22 May, IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez said: “This landmark achievement positions IMO at the forefront of regulating emerging technologies, demonstrating the Organization’s ability to anticipate and shape the future of shipping. It represents a major step forward, enabling innovation while ensuring that safety, accountability and the human element remain at the core of maritime operations.”

New approach required

A ship is considered autonomous if such shipboard technology is designed and verified to control actions without human intervention. While the number of fully crewless or remote-operated ships is currently limited, a growing number are being successfully trialled internationally.

The MASS Code introduces new requirements for the design, approval and operation of these ships, including in key areas such as navigation, connectivity, remote operations, fire safety, and search and rescue. It places strong emphasis on risk assessment, robust system design, cybersecurity and the integration of Remote Operations Centres (ROCs). Importantly, it underscores the need for human oversight, with the master retaining overall responsibility for the ship at all times – even when not on board.

Roadmap towards binding rules

The new MASS Code supplements existing IMO instruments, taking into account international law, including the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS). It is the culmination of nearly a decade of multilateral discussions, legal work and on-the-water trials, to enable new and conventional technologies to operate safely together.

The next steps for the Code include:

December 2026 – MSC 112 to re-establish MASS Working Group for the Development of a framework for an Experience-Building Phase (EBP) of the non-mandatory MASS Code;

2028 – Development of the mandatory MASS Code, based on the non-mandatory Code and results from the EBP and review conducted by the relevant sub-committees. Consideration of amendments to SOLAS (new chapter) for the Code’s adoption;

By 1 July 2030 – Expected adoption of the IMO’s first mandatory MASS Code, for entry into force on 1 January 2032.

Guidelines for ships using alternative fuels

Additionally, the Committee continued work on the safety regulatory framework for ships using new technologies and alternative fuels. It approved new Interim guidelines for the use of ammonia cargo as fuel, to support the safe design, construction and operation of ships carrying and using ammonia as fuel.

The Committee approved two new sets of interim guidelines for training seafarers on ships using alternative fuels and technologies, reflecting the need to develop new skills while addressing the specific risks of each fuel type.

text:
Japanese shipping firm NYK Line plans to issue its sixth transition bond in June 2026 as part of efforts to advance shipping decarbonisation.

The proceeds from the bonds will support projects tied to its medium-term management plan, including investments in LNG-fuelled vessels, NYK Line said in a press release on Monday.

The funding will also back other initiatives linked to its long-term vessel fuel transition strategy toward 2050.

The company had launched its first LNG-fuelled in 2016 and plans to scale up investment in LNG through 2030, before gradually moving to ammonia-fuelled ships.

NYK said the issuance builds on its sustainable finance activities, having launched the shipping industry’s first green bonds in 2018 and Japan’s first transition bonds in 2021.

Further details including the bond size and maturity will be announced later. The bonds are scheduled for issuance in early June 2026.

The transition bond framework received a second-party opinion from DNV Business Assurance Japan K.K.

title: KR Leads IMO Gas Carrier Rule Revisions, Easing Korean Shipping Burden
description:
The Korean Register (KR) has secured key amendments easing the burden on Korea's shipping and shipbuilding industries during International Maritime Organization (IMO) discussions on revising international gas carrier regulations, demonstrating its global technical competitiveness.
The newbuilding application criteria, a concern for the domestic shipbuilding industry, were also revised.
"We will continue to strengthen support so that our technical positions and industry opinions are reflected in IMO international rule discussions going forward."
"This achievement demonstrates our technical expertise in the gas carrier sector through the international rule-making process," KR Vice President Kim Kyung-bok said.

text:
The Korean Register (KR) has secured key amendments easing the burden on Korea's shipping and shipbuilding industries during International Maritime Organization (IMO) discussions on revising international gas carrier regulations, demonstrating its global technical competitiveness. Amid concerns over large-scale design changes and operational disruptions stemming from tighter rules for liquefied natural gas (LNG) carriers, KR's technical proposals have been incorporated into the final amendment, which is expected to substantially ease the cost burden on the domestic industry.

According to KR on Wednesday, the amendment to the International Code for the Construction and Equipment of Ships Carrying Liquefied Gases in Bulk (IGC Code) was finally approved at the IMO's 111th Maritime Safety Committee (MSC) meeting held in London from the 13th to 22nd. The amendment incorporates six major technical items proposed by KR.

The IGC Code is an international convention that sets structural and equipment standards for vessels carrying liquefied gases such as LNG and LPG. The IMO has been working on revisions for several years to respond to the expansion of eco-friendly ships and advances in gas carrier technology. The amendment is scheduled to be formally adopted at the 112th MSC meeting in December and will take effect on July 1, 2028.

The most notable element of the discussion was the exclusion of retroactive application of the revised pressure relief valve (PRV) standards for existing LNG carriers. Had the original amendment taken effect as drafted, an average of eight PRVs per vessel would have needed to be replaced, with additional approval and inspection procedures required, raising concerns about hundreds of millions of won in costs per ship and operational disruptions. Significant burdens were also expected for the approximately 90 LNG carriers operated by domestic shipping companies.

KR proposed to the IMO that the regulation apply only to newbuildings, and its incorporation into the final amendment helped reduce the cost burden on domestic shipping companies. Industry observers say the measure effectively eased a potential burden in the range of hundreds of billions of won.

The newbuilding application criteria, a concern for the domestic shipbuilding industry, were also revised. Previously, discussions called for the application of the revised regulations to be determined solely by the "keel-laying date." KR, along with Panama and the Active Shipbuilding Experts' Federation (ASEF), proposed a so-called "3-date criterion" that also considers the contract date and delivery date. This will help avoid confusion in which different regulations are applied to series LNG carriers of identical design.

In fact, one major domestic shipyard has voiced concerns that about half of roughly 80 already-contracted LNG carriers could fall under the strengthened regulations, raising the possibility of design changes and process delays.

KR also conducted impact analyses on a total of 97 items during the amendment discussions. It gathered opinions from the shipping and shipbuilding industries through technical seminars and information sharing, and based on this, jointly submitted an IMO amendment proposal with Korea, China, Panama and the International Association of Classification Societies (IACS).

At the IMO meeting, some member states argued for the early application of the regulations and expressed concerns about the introduction of the "3-date criterion." However, the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries and KR drew on impact analysis data and IMO guidelines to explain the technical validity and bring about an agreement.

"This is the result of the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries, KR and the domestic shipbuilding industry analyzing the impact of the amendment in advance and actively reflecting industry opinions in international discussions," said Lee Min-jung, head of the maritime safety policy division at the Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries. "We will continue to strengthen support so that our technical positions and industry opinions are reflected in IMO international rule discussions going forward."

"This achievement demonstrates our technical expertise in the gas carrier sector through the international rule-making process," KR Vice President Kim Kyung-bok said. "We will continue to provide practical technical support so that domestic shipowners and shipyards can respond stably to changes in international regulations."

title: KR, IMO 가스운반선 국제규정 개정서 기술력 '입증' - 해양통신
description:
KR은 지난 1년여간 IGC Code 전면 개정안에 포함된 총 97개 항목에 대해 적용범위, 설계영향 및 후속조치 사항 등에 대한 영향분석을 수행했다.
이후 KR은 영향분석 과정에서 식별된 기술적 쟁점을 바탕으로 4건의 IMO 개정 제안서를 마련했으며, 해당 문서들은 대한민국·중국·파나마·국제선급연합회(IACS)와 문서별 공동제출 형식으로 MSC 111에 제출됐다.
또한 KR은 국내 조선업계가 제기한 신조선 적용시점 관련 우려를 반영해, 파나마·국제조선연합회(ASEF, Active Shipbuilding Experts' Federation)를 통해 2건의 제안서를 추가로 제출했다.
아울러 KR은 97개 IGC Code 개정사항에 대한 영향분석 결과를 함께 제출하여, IMO 공식 논의의 자료로 활용되도록 했다.
KR은 MSC 111차 논의 결과를 반영하여 ‘IGC Code 개정안 영향분석 기술정보’ 문서를 개정하고 오는 7월 발간할 예정이다.
text:
KR(한국선급, 회장 이영석)은 5월 13일부터 22일까지 영국 런던에서 열린 국제해사기구(IMO, International Maritime Organization) 제111차 해사안전위원회(MSC, Maritime Safety Committee)에서 액화가스운반선에 관한 국제 협약(IGC Code, International Code for the Construction and Equipment of Ships Carrying Liquefied Gases in Bulk) 개정안이 최종 승인되었으며, 이 과정에서 KR이 제안한 주요 사항들이 개정안에 반영되었다고 26일 밝혔다.

IGC Code는 LNG, LPG 등 액화가스 운반선의 구조와 설비 등에 관한 국제규정이다.

IMO는 가스운반선 기술 발전과 친환경 선박 확대에 따라 지난 수년간 IGC Code 개정을 논의해 왔으며, 이번 개정안은 오는 12월 MSC 112차 회의에서 정식 채택된 후 2028년 7월 1일 발효될 예정이다.

KR은 지난 1년여간 IGC Code 전면 개정안에 포함된 총 97개 항목에 대해 적용범위, 설계영향 및 후속조치 사항 등에 대한 영향분석을 수행했다. 이를 바탕으로 기술정보 발행과 기술 세미나를 통해 국내 해운·조선업계 의견을 수렴하고 주요 쟁점을 도출했다.

이후 KR은 영향분석 과정에서 식별된 기술적 쟁점을 바탕으로 4건의 IMO 개정 제안서를 마련했으며, 해당 문서들은 대한민국·중국·파나마·국제선급연합회(IACS)와 문서별 공동제출 형식으로 MSC 111에 제출됐다.

주요 내용은 ▲압력도출밸브(PRV, Pressure Release Valve) 요건의 현존선 소급적용 제외 ▲선체 가열장비 비상전원 공급요건의 중복 적용 부담 완화 ▲특정 선체구조의 용접요건 개선 ▲현존선 적용 안전요건 복원 및 편집오류 정정 등이다.

특히 기존 안전기준에 따라 운용 중인 현존선 PRV에 개정요건이 소급 적용될 경우, 선박 1척당 평균 8개의 PRV 교체와 추가 승인·검사 등이 필요해, 척당 수억원의 비용과 운항 차질이 발생할 수 있는 상황이었다.

이로 인해 국내 해운선사가 운영 중인 LNG 운반선 약 90여척에 경제적인 악영향이 있을 것으로 예상됐으나, KR은 해당 규정이 신조선부터 적용되도록 제안함으로써 국내 해운선사의 경제적 부담 완화에도 상당히 기여했다.

또한 KR은 국내 조선업계가 제기한 신조선 적용시점 관련 우려를 반영해, 파나마·국제조선연합회(ASEF, Active Shipbuilding Experts' Federation)를 통해 2건의 제안서를 추가로 제출했다.

이는 개정안의 신조선 적용기준을 기존의 ‘용골거치일’ 단일 기준에서 ① 건조계약일, ② 건조계약이 없는 경우 용골거치일, ③ 선박의 인도일 순으로 판단하는 이른바 ‘3-date 기준’으로 수정할 것을 제안하는 내용으로, 우리 정부의 적극적인 지지를 통해 최종안에 반영됐다.

이에 따라 동일 설계의 시리즈 선박에 서로 다른 규정이 적용되는 문제를 해결하였다.

파악된 바에 따르면 국내 한 대형조선소는 기계약된 LNG선 약 80여척 중 절반가량이 개정 IGC Code 적용 대상이 될 수 있다고 보고, 이로 인해 설계 변경과 추가 비용 발생, 공정 지연 등의 우려를 제기한 바 있다.

아울러 KR은 97개 IGC Code 개정사항에 대한 영향분석 결과를 함께 제출하여, IMO 공식 논의의 자료로 활용되도록 했다.

특히 MSC 111 논의 과정에서는 일부 회원국이 개정안의 신속한 적용 필요성을 이유로 3-date 기준 적용에 우려를 제기했으나, 정부대표단인 해수부와 KR은 영향분석 결과와 IMO 지침을 근거로 동 기준 적용의 합리성과 기술적 타당성을 적극 설명하여 원활한 합의를 이끌었다. 이와 같이 KR의 기술 전문성과 협약 대응 경험은 국제 논의 과정에서 주요한 역할을 했다.

KR은 MSC 111차 논의 결과를 반영하여 ‘IGC Code 개정안 영향분석 기술정보’ 문서를 개정하고 오는 7월 발간할 예정이다. 여기에는 개정안 적용범위와 선사 및 조선소 후속 대응사항 등을 담을 계획이다.

MSC 111차에 대표단으로 참가한 해양수산부 해사안전정책과 이민중 과장은 “해수부와 KR, 국내 조선업계가 개정안의 영향을 사전에 분석하고, 산업계 의견을 국제 논의에 적극 반영하기 위해 협력한 결과”며, “해수부는 앞으로도 IMO 국제규정 논의에 우리나라의 기술적 입장과 산업계 의견이 효과적으로 반영될 수 있도록 지원을 강화하겠다”고 밝혔다.

KR 김경복 부사장은 “이번 성과는 KR이 가스운반선 분야의 기술적 전문성을 바탕으로 산업계의 우려를 국제 규정 논의에 효과적으로 반영한 사례”라며, “앞으로도 IMO 논의에 적극 참여하여 선주와 조선소가 국제 규정 변화에 안정적으로 대응할 수 있도록 실질적인 기술 지원을 이어가겠다”고 말했다.

MANILA (PIA) — The Philippines, through its Embassy in London, has contributed $60,000 to the International Maritime Organization to support maritime climate action, capacity-building for developing nations and expanded opportunities for women in the seafaring profession, the Philippine Embassy in London announced.

Philippine Permanent Representative to the IMO Teodoro L. Locsin Jr. presented the donation to IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez on May 18 at IMO Headquarters in London.

As one of the world’s leading providers of seafarers, the Philippines has long maintained active engagement with the IMO under the Marcos Jr. administration to advance maritime safety, security, environmental protection and sustainable shipping, interests that directly affect the livelihoods of hundreds of thousands of Filipino seafarers and their families.

The contribution was channeled through the IMO’s Integrated Technical Cooperation Program and will fund implementation of the IMO’s Strategy on Reduction of Greenhouse Gas Emissions from Shipping.

It will also support technical cooperation assistance for Small Island Developing States and Least Developed Countries, reflecting the Philippines’ commitment to solidarity with fellow developing nations.

A portion of the funds will go to the IMO’s Women in Maritime Program, which seeks to expand professional opportunities for women in an industry historically dominated by men. The Philippines noted that more Filipina women are entering the seafaring profession.

Locsin said the Philippine government remains committed to protecting the welfare of Filipino seafarers, who make up a significant share of the global maritime workforce, while also contributing to broader efforts to raise safety standards and promote inclusivity in the maritime sector.

“The Philippines recognizes the importance of contributing to global efforts that enhance maritime governance, improve safety standards, and foster fair and inclusive opportunities across the maritime sector, especially for women who want to work in this field,” Locsin said.

He also cited the Philippines’ vulnerability to climate change as a driving factor behind the country’s support for greenhouse gas reduction efforts in international shipping.

“As a climate-vulnerable country, the Philippines supports all efforts that reduce GHG emissions. By helping the IMO, we are helping not only ourselves but the entire global community in arresting the devastating effects of climate change that severely affect our own country,” Locsin said.

The Philippines currently holds a seat on the 40-member IMO Council, having been re-elected in November 2025 under Category C, which covers states with special interests in maritime transport or navigation. (JCO/PIA-NCR)
